short: EN 50600 is CENELEC's series of European Standards for data center facilities and infrastructures, with four Availability Classes and Protection Classes; CENELEC does not certify, and TSI (Trusted Site Infrastructure) is TÜViT's separate four-level certification scheme whose catalogue covers EN 50600.
title: EN 50600 and TSI, Data Center Facilities and Infrastructure
subtitle: CENELEC's European standard series for data center infrastructure, and TÜViT's TSI certification scheme
body_html:
What EN 50600 and TSI are

EN 50600 is a series of European Standards, Information technology: Data centre facilities and infrastructures, produced by CENELEC technical committee CLC/TC 215. CENELEC says its aim is to set minimum requirements for the infrastructures of data centers of every size, from a few cabinets in an existing building to dedicated multi-building sites. The series addresses the availability of the infrastructures, not the availability of the service a data center provides.

TSI (Trusted Site Infrastructure) is a separate criteria catalogue and certification scheme from TÜV Informationstechnik GmbH (TÜViT), part of the TÜV NORD Group. TÜViT says its TSI.STANDARD catalogue covers all the requirements of EN 50600 and focuses on physical security and high availability. EN 50600 is a standard; TSI is a third party's certification against its own catalogue.

What it covers

CEN-CENELEC lists these parts of the series (published editions as given in its 2024 review):

  • EN 50600-1:2019, General concepts
  • EN 50600-2-1:2021, Building construction
  • EN 50600-2-2:2019, Power supply and distribution
  • EN 50600-2-3:2019, Environmental control
  • EN 50600-2-4:2023, Telecommunications cabling infrastructure
  • EN 50600-2-5:2021, Physical security
  • EN 50600-3-1:2016, Management and operational information
  • EN 50600-4-x, key performance indicators: 4-1 overview and general requirements, 4-2 Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), 4-3 Renewable Energy Factor, 4-6 Energy Reuse Factor, 4-7 Cooling Efficiency Ratio, 4-8 Carbon Usage Effectiveness, 4-9 Water Usage Effectiveness
  • CLC/TS 50600-5-1, a maturity model for energy management and environmental sustainability with five maturity levels, and CLC/TS 50600-2-10 on earthquake risk

Availability Classes. EN 50600-2-2 (power), 2-3 (environmental control) and 2-4 (cabling) each define four Availability Classes, 1 to 4, running from low to very high. EN 50600-1 sets the overall availability of a data center at the lowest class among those three infrastructures.

Protection Classes. The series also classifies the pathways and spaces holding the infrastructure in Protection Classes, against unauthorised access and internal and external environmental events. EN 50600-2-2 and 2-3 define Protection Classes for their infrastructures, amplified in EN 50600-2-5.

International equivalent. CEN-CENELEC says ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 39 published the first editions of EN 50600-1, the 2 series and 3-1 as parts of the ISO/IEC TS 22237 series, and is developing them into full International Standards (ISO/IEC 22237-1, -2, -3, -4 and -6 so far).

How a claim is made and checked

CENELEC does not certify data centers. The CEN/CLC/ETSI Coordination Group on Green Data Centres says the EN 50600 series does not define a conformity assessment procedure. Conformity can be shown by self-declaration by the owner or operator, or by a third-party assessment. It also says that, lacking a true certification system for data centres, both approaches have equal technical status, and that self-declaration, not formal certification, is all that is available. A third party offering such services has to be accredited against the EN ISO/IEC 17000 series by an accreditation body.

TÜViT offers certification against its TSI catalogue. Its fact sheet describes the project phases: an optional workshop, document review, a certification audit with site inspection, a report, the certification decision and publication of the certificate, and a full re-certification after 24 months. TSI certificates are awarded at four levels:

  • Level 1, medium availability
  • Level 2, extended availability
  • Level 3, high availability
  • Level 4, highest availability

The TSI criteria cover environment, construction, fire protection, security systems, cabling, power supply, cooling, organisation and documentation, and dual-site data centers.

What a claim does not mean

  • "EN 50600 certified" is not a CENELEC certificate. CENELEC publishes the standard; any certificate comes from a third party such as TÜViT, or the claim is a self-declaration.
  • An Availability Class describes the design of the infrastructure, not the uptime a customer will get. CENELEC says the series addresses infrastructure availability, not service availability.
  • A TSI level is TÜViT's rating against its own catalogue. It is not the same scale as Uptime Institute Tiers or TIA-942 Rated levels.
  • A TSI certificate is time limited: TÜViT requires a full re-certification after 24 months.

In data centers

A claim usually concerns one facility. A reader should check whether it is a self-declaration or a third-party certificate; for a certificate, the certifying body, the scheme (TSI.STANDARD level, or an EN 50600 Availability Class and Protection Classes), the site covered, and the issue and expiry dates. A claim of "EN 50600 Class 3" is a statement about the lowest-rated of the power, environmental control and cabling infrastructures.

Related standards

Other ways of rating a facility's design are Uptime Institute Tier Certification and ANSI/TIA-942. The EN 50600-4 KPIs are used in the EU Code of Conduct for Data Centres and the Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact.
